The evolution of work

The history of people, work, and evidence.

Human resource management did not begin with an algorithm. Its story brings together the organization of labor, the psychology of work, employee rights and the ways we try to learn from evidence.

Explore twelve overlapping chapters, from early labor organization to foundation models. Each connects an important development to psychology, measurement, and the questions researchers can test today.

Psychology

What are we trying to understand?

Motivation, fairness, safety and well-being are constructs that need careful definition and validation—not labels to infer from arbitrary data.

Analytics

What can the evidence support?

Surveys, historical records and models answer different questions. Prediction alone does not establish a cause or represent every worker's experience.

People & rights

Who benefits and who decides?

Employee voice, privacy, labor rights and unequal power shape whether research is trustworthy and appropriate.

This is a selected narrative with a US and European emphasis, not a complete global history. Periods overlap. The psychological concepts shown here are research lenses, not diagnoses or validated PeopleFM findings.

From historical work to available data

The original data behind historical studies are not all public, machine-readable, or comparable. The experiments below use two separately sourced datasets to explore the later prediction question; they do not recreate Hawthorne, engagement, or psychological-safety studies.

RESEARCH IN PROGRESS

The central question remains open.

Two exploratory, local comparisons now include conventional models and TabICLv2. One uses fictional records; the other uses a small subsample of a TabArena job-search-intention dataset. Neither establishes operational effectiveness.

Scope: offline research and aggregate analysis, never individual employment decisions.

The research question

Transfer is a claim to test.

Limited labels

Compare performance across prespecified training-set fractions, using the same held-out examples and repeated subsampling.

PROPOSED

Distribution shift

Evaluate independent, compatible organizations and time periods. Random splits alone cannot establish generalization.

PROPOSED

Multiple outcomes

Compare shared representations with task-specific baselines only when legitimate, distinct targets are available.

PROPOSED

Shared-dataset experiments · locally executed

Traditional models meet a foundation model.

Every model shown for a dataset used the same fixed training and test rows. Select a dataset and metric to inspect the measured results. These are exploratory experiments, not a reproduction of the published TabArena leaderboard.

Start with the context. The IBM sample is fictional. The TabArena dataset records job-search intention, not actual turnover. Neither experiment establishes real-world employment performance or supports individual decisions.

ModelROC-AUC95% bootstrap intervalPrediction timeStatus

Intervals resample test rows with class counts fixed and condition on each fitted model; they do not capture training or tuning variation. Single-split intervals are not a statistical test of model differences. Prediction time is for the entire held-out batch on one machine and depends on hardware and implementation. Preprocessing time is excluded for TabICLv2.

How the comparison was made

Logistic regression, random forest, MLP, XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost were tuned by repeated stratified cross-validation inside the training split. The pretrained TabICLv2 model used one ensemble member without task-specific fine-tuning. Models therefore have different compute budgets. Imputation, encoding and scaling were fitted only on training data; classification metrics use a threshold fixed at 0.5.

TabArena’s 2025 benchmark paper and the 2026 TabICLv2 paper use a much broader suite, repeated evaluation and different configurations. Our bounded run is on one selected subset and does not reproduce their protocol or scores.

Inside the foundation model

How TabICLv2 learns in context.

The official model is pretrained on many synthetic prediction tasks. During inference it receives a table of labeled training examples as context and predicts held-out rows with frozen weights. Our experiment uses the official classification checkpoint, one ensemble member, and CPU execution; it does not train a new PeopleFM foundation model.

1 · Feature & target embeddingTraining labels inform feature representations; test labels stay hidden
2 · Column encoderInduced attention models each feature across rows
3 · Row encoderAttention combines features; four CLS tokens summarize each row
4 · In-context predictionTest-row representations attend to labeled training context

Column-wise embedding

For classification, the paper describes three induced self-attention blocks, 128 inducing vectors, dimension 128 and eight heads. Target-aware embeddings add training-label information to feature representations.

Feature interaction

A three-layer row transformer with four learned CLS tokens produces a 512-dimensional row representation by concatenating their outputs.

Dataset-wise learning

A 12-layer transformer processes row embeddings. Test rows attend to training rows; a prediction head produces class outputs. Scalable softmax is designed to help with longer contexts.

Conceptual flow: zᵢ = RowEncoder(ColumnEncoder(xᵢ, context labels));   p(y* | x*, context) = Head(ICL(z*, ztrain, ytrain)).

The equation is a schematic, not a complete implementation. Model details and pretraining are described in the TabICLv2 paper, sections 3–5 and appendix A. Our preprocessing and single-member execution differ from its reported benchmark setup.

Experiment lab

Reproducibility starts locally.

The repository contains a Python benchmark command for a locally acquired CSV. It creates a held-out test split, tunes on training folds and writes aggregate metrics and metadata.

Research publication

A protocol with an honest boundary.

Abstract. We investigate whether tabular foundation models offer practical advantages over conventional models under label scarcity, shift and multiple tasks. Current evidence remains insufficient to answer this question. We report two exploratory, locally executed comparisons, including a fictional dataset and a bounded TabArena subsample; neither tests cross-organization transfer.

Limitations and responsible use

The fictional IBM sample is not a real workforce; the TabArena job-change target is intention rather than actual attrition. Prediction is not causation, sensitive attributes can have proxies, and individual scores must not be used for employment decisions. Meaningful claims need documented data provenance, temporal validity, uncertainty, privacy safeguards and subgroup evaluation.
